⚡ The 60-Second Cheat Sheet

1. Softwood vs Hardwood — the ONE thing to know

SoftwoodHardwood
TreeConiferous (cone-bearing) — needlesDeciduous — broad leaves
LeavesStay on all year (evergreen)Fall off in winter
GrowthFast — 20+ years to matureSlow — 100+ years
ClimateCool temperate regionsWarmer regions
ExamplesPine, Cedar, Redwood, SpruceMahogany, Oak, Beech, Jelutong, Meranti, Balsa
⚠️ Don't fall for the name: "hardwood" does NOT mean the wood is hard! Balsa is a HARDWOOD and it's the softest, lightest wood of all. The category is about the tree type, not the wood's hardness.

2. Wood ID — appearance → name (the classic exam question)

WoodCategoryAppearanceKey propertiesUses
PineSoftwoodYellowish, long thick grainLow densityConstruction, cheap furniture
CedarSoftwoodLight red-brown, turns silverNatural preservatives, deters insectsClothing storage, outdoor construction
RedwoodSoftwoodRich reddish-brown, subtle light age ringsLightweight but durable, resists water & decayOutdoor furniture & decking, fine woodworking
SpruceSoftwoodLight yellow grain, long thick grainExcellent strength-to-weight ratioConstruction, pulp for paper
MahoganyHardwoodLight red/brown, darkens by ageStable (doesn't warp), highly workableFine furniture, musical instruments
OakHardwoodSwirly grain, medium darknessHigh density, durableHigh-quality furniture, tall ships
BeechHardwoodLight colour, small dashes/frecklesAntiseptic, doesn't splinterChildren's toys, kitchenware & handles
JelutongHardwoodUniform pale white, straight grainLightweight, non-durableWood carving, stationery, matchsticks
MerantiHardwoodRich colour, ribbon stripe grainLow warping, easy to workBudget furniture, doors & windows
BalsaHardwoodVery light, soft, swirly grainVery low density, easily damagedModelling, prototypes
Exam technique: the question shows a photo + asks "name this wood & give two properties". Use the appearance clues (colour + grain pattern) to name it, then quote properties, then a use. 1 mark each — don't write essays.

3. Structure of wood — 3 facts that always come up

  • Trees carry water up through xylem tubes (fibres).
  • From the side, the tubes show as dark lines = grain. Wood is weak along the grain.
  • Dark rings = age rings — count them to age a tree. Dark rings form from slow winter growth (denser).

4. Manufactured boards — one line each

BoardMade fromKey facts
MDFFine wood particles + glue compressedVery dense, can't get wet, flakes apart
PlywoodLayers of ply glued at 90° each layerGrain alternated to remove weakness; different quality layers possible
BlockboardSoftwood strips core + ply top & bottomUse when you need thicker material
ChipboardLarge wood particles + glue compressedCheapest wood product; normally covered with laminate

5. Preparation & stock forms

  • Wood must be dried to 10–20% water content: stabilises it + kills fungus/insects.
  • Air drying: 8–16 months, reduces cracking & twisting. Kiln drying: 6–8 weeks, quick & cost-effective.
  • Stock forms: Plank · Strip · Square · Veneer · Dowel (dowels have grooves so glue can grip).
  • Boards bigger than a tree = glue planks together with sash clamps, alternating grain curve direction so twisting doesn't multiply.

6. Shaping — tools in one glance

JobHand toolsMachines
Cut straight linesTenon saw, panel saw (big sheets)Bandsaw, circular saw, scroll saw (curves)
Cut curvesCoping sawScroll saw
Remove bulkSaws → then file/sand/planeBelt/disc sander
Flat surfacesJack / jointer / smoothing plane—
HolesHand drill, bradawlPillar drill
Recesses/mouldingChisels (bevel, mortise, gouge)Router, mortise cutter, wood lathe
Hold workBench hook—
Saw blade rules: thick blade = straight cuts, thin blade = curves. Small teeth = harder materials, large teeth remove more material quickly.

7. Joining — the marks-heavy section

  • Adhesives: Epoxy resin (2-part, 10 min, thermoset) · Cascamite (waterproof, 3 h, strong) · PVA (2 h, sets clear, soaks into fibres) · Acrylic cement (1 min, solvent, capillary action — plastic) · Contact adhesive (15 min, goes tacky then pressed together).
  • Joints: butt, cross halving, finger, mortise & tenon, mitre, lap, dowel, dovetail, housing. Terminology: halving (corner/bridle/tee), through vs blind, tongue & groove, biscuit joint, rebate.
  • Knock-down fittings (flat-pack, e.g. IKEA): corner blocks, scan fitting, cam lock, modesty block — assemble with just a screwdriver/Allen key.
  • Screws: pilot hole (stops splitting) → clearance hole (lets outer panel slide) → countersink (head sits flush).
  • Nails: dovetail (angled, won't pull out) · staggered (prevents splitting down grain) · clinch (end bent over).

8. Construction, production & jigs

  • Frame construction = narrow boards joined (mortise & tenon). Carcase construction = solid box of panels joined end-to-end (lap joints).
  • Production: one-off (1, skilled, expensive) → batch (4–50, jigs) → mass (1000+, production line) → continuous (never stops, e.g. paper).
  • Mould = material flows INTO the cavity · Former = soft material pulled OVER the shape · Drilling jig = locates holes accurately & quickly · Holding device = holds & lines up material.

9. Finishing

  • Abrasive papers: glass paper / aluminium oxide paper — used to finish woods, multiple grades (coarse → fine).
  • Finishes (from the deck): varnishes, oils, waxes, paints/stains — protect the wood and improve appearance. (Full detail in the Finishing tab.)

⭐ How to Get A* — the step-by-step path

Step 1 — Learn the ID tables (Week 1)

Photos of all 10 woods + 4 boards until you can name any sample in seconds. Use the photos in the Woods tab: cover the name, say appearance → properties → uses. 30 min a day for a week = done.

Step 2 — Learn the process chains (Week 2)

For each stage — preparation → marking out → shaping → joining → finishing — be able to list the tools/machines and say why each step exists. Questions love "why do we dry wood / why a pilot hole / why alternate grain in plywood".

Step 3 — Joint scoring + terminology (Week 3)

This is the most predictable exam question: score 4–6 joints on aesthetics / surface area / mechanical strength / difficulty. Memorise your benchmark scores (see Joining tab) so you can fill the table fast.

Step 4 — Command words & past papers (Week 4+)

Learn what state/name/describe/explain/suggest want (Exam Skills tab), then do past Paper 2s timed. Timed past papers = the single highest-impact revision (1–2 grade improvement).

🌲 Woods & Boards — full detail

CategoriesStructureSoftwoodsHardwoodsManufactured boards

What are the categories of wood?

Wood comes from two types of tree — the tree type decides the category, not how hard the wood is.

🌲 Softwood🍂 Hardwood
Tree typeConiferous (cone-bearing)Deciduous (broad-leaf)
LeavesStay on all yearFall off in the winter
Growth speedFast — 20+ yearsSlow — 100+ years
Where foundCool temperate regionsWarmer regions
ExamplesPine, Cedar, Redwood, SpruceMahogany, Oak, Beech, Jelutong, Meranti, Balsa
💡 Because softwoods grow fast, they're cheaper and more sustainable — forests regrow on short rotations. Hardwoods grow slowly, so they're more expensive and scarcer.

What is the structure of wood?

  • Trees use tubes (xylem) to transport water up the tree — we call these fibres.
  • From the side, the fibres show as dark lines — this is the grain.
  • Wood is weak along the grain. (Classic exam question: "How will this break?" — answer: it splits along the grain, following the fibres.)
  • You can count the dark rings on a tree to determine its age — these are age rings.
  • The dark lines are denser and formed from slow growth during winter; light rings are fast summer growth.

Balsa is actually the LIGHTEST, softest wood. Ask your teacher which they want in the exam; the photo in the deck shows the real balsa sample.

Manufactured boards

Manufactured board is a composite material made from wood particles, fibres and veneers bound together with adhesives to create a wood-like panel.

  • Advantages: improved properties — directional strength, stable dimensions, cheaper, uniform, stable.
  • Disadvantages: some are easily damaged or soak up water; some weigh more or cost more.

MDF (Medium Density Fibreboard)

  • Wood particles and glue compressed together.
  • Can't get wet — it swells.
  • Very dense.
  • Will flake apart (edges crumble).

Plywood

  • Layers of ply with the grain glued together at 90 degrees each time — this removes the weakness (wood is weak along the grain, so alternate the direction).
  • Different quality materials can be used (e.g. decorative outer veneer, cheap core).

Blockboard

  • Strips of softwood in the core with a layer of ply on the top and bottom.
  • Useful when you need thicker material without the weight/cost of solid wood.

Chipboard

  • Large wood particles and glue compressed together.
  • The cheapest wood product you can buy.
  • Normally covered with laminate (e.g. flat-pack shelves).

🪵 Preparation of woods

Environmental impactsDryingStock formsMaking boards

Environmental impacts — softwood vs hardwood

🌲 Softwoods (good for the environment)

  • Fast growth rates: forests replenished and harvested on a shorter, sustainable rotation.
  • Carbon sequestration: growing trees absorb CO₂, locking it into the wood fibre for the product's whole lifecycle.
  • Lower energy processing: sawmills burn leftover green residues (bark, sawdust) on site to power kiln-drying and machinery — less fossil fuel.

🍂 Hardwoods (slower, more impact)

  • Slow growth cycles: hardwood trees take decades or centuries to mature — slow to replace.
  • Harvesting mature hardwoods removes carbon sinks that took 100+ years to build.
  • Often transported long distances (tropical hardwoods) — higher embodied energy.
  • Choose certified/sustainable sources where possible.

Why do we need to dry wood?

  • Reduces the water content to 10–20%.
  • Stabilises the wood (stops warping/twisting/shrinking after you build with it).
  • Kills fungus and insects.
Air dryingKiln drying
HowStacked outdoors with spacers, coveredControlled heated chamber
Time8–16 months6–8 weeks
ProsReduces cracking and twisting (gentler)Quick and cost-effective

Stock forms — standard material profiles

💡 Dowels have grooves along their length — the grooves allow excess glue to escape and grip when the dowel is pushed into a hole. Exam love this detail.

Creating boards from planks

  • Planks can only be as big as the tree allows — so you glue multiple planks together to make a board.
  • Sash clamps are used to glue large pieces together.
  • Natural woods bend and twist — when you glue planks into a board, the bending could multiply.
  • So you glue the curve of the grain in alternating directions — each plank's twist cancels the next one out.

📏 Marking out

EquipmentMethodsWorking face & edgeFPT — finger joint

Types of marking-out equipment

ToolWhat it's for
Metal ruleMeasuring, drawing straight lines, checking flatness
Try squareMarking and checking 90° (square) corners
Marking gaugeScoring a line parallel to an edge, at a set distance
Marking knifePrecise cut line; also creates a track that stops saws/chisels wandering and prevents splitting beyond the line
Mitre squareMarking 45° mitre angles
Sliding bevelMarking and transferring any angle
BradawlTwisting a small starter hole so screws start straight
Mortise gaugeTwo adjustable pins — marks both sides of a mortise at once

Marking-out methods

  • Mark out on all sides — keeps cutting accurate and square (you can see the line from every direction).
  • Shade out waste material (scribble over it) — shows exactly where to cut and stops you cutting the wrong piece.
  • Marking knives are used for precision — the knife line also creates a track for saws and chisels, and prevents wood splitting beyond the line.

Working face & working edge

A board's working face and working edge are the two reference surfaces that all measurements are taken from.

  • This dates back to when boards were planed by hand — you couldn't rely on every side being parallel, so two surfaces were designated as reference surfaces.
  • It's still a good idea today. The marks can also mean front and top.
  • Everything is measured from the working face/edge, so a mistake never propagates from an uneven surface.

FPT — Mark out a finger joint

Teacher instruction: Mark out a finger joint on the wood (x / ¼y / y dimensions on the side profile).

  1. Mark all the way around the wood — this helps when you cut it out.
  2. Scribble the waste material — prevents cutting the wrong piece.
  3. Transfer the profile from the end face down both sides so saw cuts line up.
The finger joint has a large surface area for glue → strong + looks like interlocking fingers. Cutting it accurately = mark both sides, cut just on the waste side of the line, then trim to the line with a chisel.

🪚 Shaping woods

SawsChiselsPlanesMachinesHand machinesLaminating & steamingFPT — laminated organiser

Cutting — saws

Saws are used to remove the bulk of the material close to shape — then a metal file, sandpaper or planes give the final shape and finish.

Blade / teethRule
Thick bladesFor straight cuts (stiff, won't flex off line)
Thin bladesFor curved cuts (can follow the curve)
Smaller teethFor harder materials (finer cut)
Large teethRemove more material quickly

Types of chisels

⚠️ Keep both hands on/behind the chisel. Never put a hand in front of the cutting edge — a slip will push the blade into your hand. Push with the palm, guide with the other hand behind.

Types of wood planes

💡 How a plane works: the base sits on the high spots; the plane blade cuts the high spots off until the surface is flat.

Types of woodworking machines

MachineJob
Belt sanderFast flat sanding of large surfaces
Disc sanderSanding end grain and small parts to a line
Scroll sawIntricate curves and internal cut-outs
Pillar drillAccurate, repeatable vertical holes
BandsawCutting thick stock, straight or gentle curves
Mortise cutterSquare/rectangular slots for mortise & tenon joints
Wood latheTurning cylindrical/spindle shapes

Types of woodworking hand machines (power tools)

Laminating and steaming

Steaming (bending)

  • Problem: cutting a curved shape out of a solid board wastes material and is weak across the grain.
  • Steaming softens the resin in the wood, which allows it to be bent while soft.
  • Steam chamber: wood is left in hot steam until the resin softens, then bent around a former/jig and left to set.

Laminating

  • Thin/flexible pieces of wood are glued together and held in shape; when the glue sets, it stays in that shape.
  • Vacuum bag — uses air pressure to hold the laminate in shape.
  • A jig — uses clamps to hold it in shape.
Exam difference: steaming bends ONE piece of solid wood (resin softened by heat/steam). Laminating bends MANY thin pieces glued together. Both need a former/jig to hold the shape while setting.

FPT — Laminated Organiser

Teacher instruction: Choose one of these products. Create a blue foam former and laminate using the bagpress.

  1. Choose your product design (organiser).
  2. Create a blue foam former — the foam is shaped to the curve you want, then the flexible plywood is pressed over/into it.
  3. Laminate using the bagpress (vacuum bag) — air pressure holds the plies tight to the former.
  4. Remember: flexible plywood will only bend to a maximum radius before breaking — design your former curve within the limit.
  5. Finish the edge of the product using a jack plane.

🔩 Joining & assembly

AdhesivesJointsScoring jointsTerminologyKnock-down fittingsScrewsNailsConstructionProductionJigs, formers, mouldsFPTs

Types of adhesives

AdhesiveTypeGluing timeKey facts
Epoxy resinGeneral purpose10 minutes2-part adhesive (resin + hardener); a type of thermoset plastic
CascamiteWaterproof glue3 hoursStrong wood glue; for outdoor/marine use
PVAGeneral purpose wood glue2 hoursNeeds to soak into the wood fibres; sets clear
Acrylic cementPlastic glue1 minuteSolvent — evaporates; uses capillary action to flow into the joint
Contact adhesiveGeneral purpose15 minutesAllow surfaces to go tacky before joining; bonds instantly on contact
Exam questions pair adhesives with materials: wood → PVA/Cascamite · plastic → acrylic cement · anything strong/waterproof → epoxy. Quote the gluing time to show you know the difference.

Types of joints

The class deck shows photo grids of joints. Learn to recognise each one by shape:

JointWhat it looks like / how it works
Butt jointTwo square ends pushed together; weakest — relies on glue
Cross halvingBoth pieces halved (half-thickness cut) and crossed over, flush
Finger jointInterlocking rectangular fingers; big glue surface; strong
Mortise & tenonTenon (tongue) on one piece fits a mortise (slot) in the other; classic frame joint
Mitre jointBoth ends cut at 45° meeting at a corner; neat, weak, needs reinforcement
Lap jointOne piece lapped over another, half-thickness; simple & strong-ish
Dowel jointHoles + dowels align two pieces; hidden, quick with jigs
Dovetail jointFan-shaped pins + tails; very strong, can't pull apart; hard to make
Housing jointSlot (housing) cut across one board; shelf fits into it

The deck sets up this exact exam-style question:

Score each joint for the following (out of 10): Aesthetics · Surface Area (for glue) · Mechanical strength · Difficulty to construct.
JointAesthetics /10Surface area /10Mechanical strength /10Difficulty /10
Butt joint2121
Cross halving joint4454
Finger joint7886
Mortise & tenon joint7697
Mitre joint8335
Lap joint4563
Dowel joint8564

How to answer these in the exam: pick 2–3 joints and justify each score with ONE reason, e.g. "Finger joint — high surface area gives a strong glue bond" / "Butt joint — end grain glues poorly and there's little surface area, so it's weak." Justify = the marks.

Joint terminology — random questions found in exams

TermMeaning
HalvingBoth pieces cut to half thickness where they cross, so they sit flush
CornerHalving joint at a corner (L shape)
BridleLike a halving but one piece keeps full thickness with a slot for the other (open mortise & tenon)
TeeHalving joint forming a T shape
ThroughJoint that goes all the way through the piece (visible on both faces)
BlindJoint that stops inside the piece (hidden from the outside)
Tongue & grooveRidge (tongue) on one edge slides into a slot (groove) on the other — for edge-joining boards
Biscuit jointSmall oval "biscuit" of compressed wood fits slots in both pieces; swells with glue to lock
RebateStep/recess cut along the edge of a board (like a half-thickness ledge)

Knock-down fittings

Knock-down fittings are hardware components designed to join panels together temporarily or permanently without traditional wood glue and clamps.

They're heavily used in flat-pack furniture (e.g. IKEA) — manufactured quickly, shipped flat, assembled at home with basic tools like a screwdriver or Allen key.

FittingWhat it does
Corner blockSmall triangular block screwed into a corner to stiffen it
Scan fittingMetal barrel + bolt that pulls two panels together
Cam lockDowel/bolt head locks into a rotating cam — the classic IKEA fitting
Modesty blockHidden block that reinforces a joint/panel corner

Using screws

  1. Drill a pilot hole through outer and inner panels — diameter slightly bigger than the core of the screw; prevents the wood splitting.
  2. Drill a clearance hole in the outer panel — diameter of the threads; stops the screw gripping the outer panel so it pulls both panels together.
  3. Drill a countersink — angled hole so the head lies flush with the surface.
  4. Insert the screw with a manual screwdriver (controlled torque).
Common exam trap: mixing up pilot and clearance. Pilot = core diameter, both panels, stops splitting. Clearance = thread diameter, outer panel only, lets the screw pull panels together.

Types of nails

PatternWhy
Dovetail nailingAngling the nails (opposite directions) so they don't pull out
Staggered nailingOffset nails so they don't split the wood down the grain
Clinch nailingBending the end of the nail over to prevent it falling out
💡 Choose nail length: a nail should be about 2–2.5× the thickness of the top piece, so it bites deep into the lower piece without poking through.

Types of construction — frame vs carcase

Frame construction

Uses interconnected narrow boards joined by profiles like mortise & tenon. Light, strong for its weight — tables, chairs, doors.

Carcase construction

Builds a solid box using panels joined end-to-end like lap joints. Strong and enclosed — cabinets, drawers, wardrobes.

Types of production

TypeVolumeSkillTools/machinesNotes
One-off1 product at a timeHighly skilledNon-specific tools & machinesExpensive to produce (e.g. bespoke furniture)
Batch4–50 productsMedium skilledNon-specific tools + use of jigs; multiple identical machinese.g. school FPT products
Mass1000+ productsLow skilledSpecific machines; production linese.g. consumer furniture
ContinuousContinuously producedLow skilledSpecific machines; production linesNever stops (e.g. paper, plywood)
💡 The level of production depends on: volume needed, cost of setup, and how much customisation the customer requires.

Jigs, formers, moulds

DeviceDefinition
MouldMaterial flows into the cavity (casting)
FormerSoft material is pulled over the shape (bending/laminating)
Drilling jigHelps locate the hole accurately and quickly — repeatable
Holding deviceHolds and lines up material while you work

FPTs — practical tasks from the deck

FPT — Knock-down fittings (pairs)

Teacher instruction: In pairs, using scrap wood, make the drilling jigs and construct a scan fitting.

  1. Question to solve first: how would you make a drilling jig to drill these holes? — a jig guarantees the same hole positions on every identical piece.
  2. Make the drilling jig from scrap wood.
  3. Drill the holes and assemble the scan fitting.

FPT — Screws and Nails (paired activity)

Teacher instruction: Follow the steps to create a countersunk screw joint. Then, using 4 nails, try dovetail nailing.

  1. Mark and drill pilot + clearance + countersink holes.
  2. Drive the countersunk screw flush.
  3. Practice dovetail nailing: 4 nails, angled so they lock.

🖌️ Finishing woods

Abrasive papersFinishes

Abrasive papers

  • Glass paper / aluminium oxide paper — used to finish woods.
  • Available in multiple grades (grit numbers): coarse (low number, e.g. 80) removes material fast; fine (high number, e.g. 400) smooths.
  • Work through grades coarse → fine; always sand with the grain for the final pass.

Finishes

Finishes protect the wood (moisture, scratches, insects) and improve appearance. Common finish types:

FinishLooks / feelUse for
VarnishClear, glossy or satin, tough filmFurniture, outdoor wood, floors
Danish oil / linseed oilNatural look, soaks into grainHandles, chopping boards, bare wood look
Wax polishSoft sheen, feels smoothFurniture upkeep (over other finishes)
Wood stainChanges colour, grain still visibleCheap wood made to look like oak/walnut
Paint / lacquerOpaque coloured filmProtection + colour, toys, metal-look items
Process: sand with graded abrasives → dust off → apply finish in thin coats → rub down between coats with fine abrasive → final coat.

📝 Exam skills — scoring on Paper 2

Command words"Identify the wood" questionsJoint scoring questionsFPT strategyCommon mistakesGlossaryQuiz

Command words decoded

CommandWhat the examiner wantsMarks usually
State / NameOne word / short phrase. No explanation needed.1 each
ListSeveral short items, one per mark1 each
DescribeSay WHAT something looks like / how it's done — factual2–4
ExplainSay WHY — cause and effect. "Because…" answers earn the mark2–4
SuggestUse your knowledge creatively; any sensible justified answer accepted2–6
Evaluate / CompareBoth sides + a justified conclusion4–8
"Describe the appearance of this wood" ≠ "Explain why it's used for X". Describe = facts you can see; Explain = reasons. Read the command word before writing.

"Identify the wood" questions

Photo of a wood sample + "Name this wood. Give two properties and one use." (4 marks)

  1. Appearance clues: colour (yellowish = pine, red-brown = cedar/mahogany, pale white = jelutong/balsa) + grain (long thick = softwoods, swirly = oak, ribbon stripe = meranti, freckles = beech).
  2. Category: say softwood or hardwood too — often a mark.
  3. Properties: quote the deck table (density, durability, workability, water resistance).
  4. Use: connect to properties — e.g. cedar repels insects → clothing storage.
Never write "it's hard/soft" as a property of hardwood/softwood — Balsa is a hardwood and is soft! Say density, durability, stability, workability instead.

Joint scoring questions

"Score each joint for aesthetics, surface area, mechanical strength and difficulty to construct. Justify one of your scores."

  1. Fill the table fast using your benchmarks (Joining tab).
  2. Justification = property → consequence: "Finger joint has a large surface area, so the glue bond is strong."
  3. Relate to use: "A dovetail can't be pulled apart, so it suits drawers."

FPT (Focused Practical Task) strategy

FPTs are the timed practicals: finger joint, laminated organiser, KD fitting + drilling jig, screws & nails. Marks come from process, not the finished look.

StageWhat earns marks
Marking outLines on ALL sides; waste shaded; working face/edge used; accurate to the line
CuttingCut on waste side of line; square cuts; appropriate saw; work held (bench hook)
ShapingPlanes/chisels used correctly; both hands behind chisel; grain direction respected
JoiningPilot/clearance/countersink for screws; correct adhesive & clamping; joint square
FinishingSanded through grades with grain; finish applied evenly
Safety & cleanupGoggles, guards, safe posture, bench cleaned — always marked
Time plan: 20% marking out, 40% cutting/shaping, 30% joining/finishing, 10% check. If you're behind, a clean square joint beats a decorated rough one.

Common mistakes (lose marks here)

  • ✗ Saying hardwood = hard. Tree type decides the category.
  • ✗ Mixing pilot vs clearance hole diameters.
  • ✗ "Describe" answers written as "Explain" (no because).
  • ✗ Forgetting wood is weak along the grain in break/strength questions.
  • ✗ Naming MDF for outdoor use — it can't get wet.
  • ✗ Writing "glue" instead of a named adhesive with its properties.
  • ✗ No justification in the joint scoring table.

Glossary — 60+ terms

Softwood
Wood from coniferous (evergreen, cone-bearing) trees; grows fast (20+ yrs).
Hardwood
Wood from deciduous (broad-leaf) trees that lose leaves in winter; grows slowly (100+ yrs).
Deciduous
Tree that sheds its leaves in winter.
Coniferous
Cone-bearing, evergreen tree (needles).
Xylem
Tubes (fibres) that transport water up the tree.
Fibres
The tube structures in wood; seen as grain from the side.
Grain
The dark lines of fibres in wood; wood is weak along the grain.
Age rings
Dark rings (winter growth) counted to age a tree.
Manufactured board
Composite panel of wood particles/fibres/veneers + adhesive (MDF, plywood, blockboard, chipboard).
MDF
Medium-density fibreboard; fine particles + glue; dense; damaged by water.
Plywood
Layers glued with grain alternating 90° to remove weakness.
Blockboard
Softwood strip core with ply faces; for thick material.
Chipboard
Large particles + glue; cheapest board; usually laminated.
Veneer
Ultra-thin slice of wood for surfacing cheaper boards.
Dowel
Round wooden rod; grooved so glue grips in a hole.
Stock form
Standard profile a material is sold in (plank, strip, square, veneer, dowel).
Kiln drying
Drying wood in a controlled heated chamber; 6–8 weeks.
Air drying
Slow outdoor drying; 8–16 months; reduces cracking/twisting.
Working face / edge
The two reference surfaces all measurements are taken from.
Try square
Tool to mark/check 90° corners.
Marking gauge
Tool scoring a line parallel to an edge.
Marking knife
Knife for precise lines; creates a track for saws/chisels, prevents splitting.
Mitre square
Tool for marking 45° angles.
Sliding bevel
Adjustable tool for marking any angle.
Bradawl
Pointed tool making starter holes for screws.
Mortise gauge
Two-pin gauge marking mortise width.
Tenon saw
Saw for straight cuts (stiff blade, fine teeth).
Coping saw
Saw for curves (thin blade in a frame).
Panel saw
Large saw for cutting sheets.
Bench hook
Device that holds work against the bench for sawing.
Bevel chisel
General-purpose chisel.
Mortise chisel
Thick strong chisel for chopping mortises.
Gouge
Curved chisel for concave shapes.
Jack plane
General flattening plane.
Jointer plane
Long plane for true edges.
Smoothing plane
Plane for final smoothing.
Spoke shave
Small plane for curved edges.
Pillar drill
Machine for accurate vertical holes.
Bandsaw
Machine saw for thick stock, straight or curves.
Scroll saw
Machine for fine curves/internal cut-outs.
Mortise cutter
Machine that chops mortise slots.
Wood lathe
Machine turning round/spindle shapes.
Router
Power tool for grooves, rebates, mouldings.
Jigsaw
Portable power saw for curves.
Steaming
Softening resin with steam so solid wood can bend.
Steam chamber
Enclosure where wood is steamed before bending.
Laminating
Gluing thin flexible layers and holding them in shape until set.
Vacuum bag
Air pressure holds laminates in shape.
Former
Shape soft material is pulled OVER.
Mould
Cavity material flows INTO.
Drilling jig
Device locating holes accurately/repeatably.
Holding device
Device that holds and lines up material.
Epoxy resin
2-part thermoset adhesive; 10 min gluing time.
Cascamite
Waterproof wood glue; 3 h; strong.
PVA
General wood glue; 2 h; soaks into fibres; sets clear.
Acrylic cement
Solvent plastic glue; 1 min; capillary action.
Contact adhesive
Glue applied to both surfaces, left tacky, then pressed together.
Thermoset
Plastic that sets irreversibly when cured (e.g. epoxy).
Butt joint
Square ends glued together; weakest joint.
Cross halving
Both pieces half-thickness, crossed flush.
Finger joint
Interlocking rectangular fingers; large glue area.
Mortise & tenon
Tenon in a mortise slot; classic strong frame joint.
Mitre joint
45° corners meeting; neat but weak.
Lap joint
Half-thickness overlap joint.
Dowel joint
Holes + dowels aligning two pieces.
Dovetail joint
Fan-shaped pins/tails; very strong, cannot pull apart.
Housing joint
Slot cut across a board to take a shelf.
Bridle joint
Open slot joint; like an open mortise & tenon.
Tongue & groove
Ridge-in-slot edge joint for boards.
Biscuit joint
Oval compressed-wood biscuit swelling in slots to lock boards.
Rebate
Step recess cut along a board edge.
Through joint
Joint visible on both faces.
Blind joint
Hidden joint, stops inside the material.
Knock-down fitting
Hardware joining panels without glue/clamps (flat-pack furniture).
Cam lock
Rotating cam + bolt KD fitting (IKEA).
Corner block
Triangular block stiffening a corner.
Modesty block
Hidden block reinforcing a joint.
Scan fitting
Metal barrel + bolt KD fitting.
Pilot hole
Hole at screw-core diameter preventing splitting.
Clearance hole
Hole at thread diameter in the outer panel.
Countersink
Angled recess letting the screw head sit flush.
Dovetail nailing
Angled nails that resist pulling out.
Staggered nailing
Offset nails avoiding splits down the grain.
Clinch nailing
Nail end bent over to lock it.
Frame construction
Narrow boards joined by profiles (mortise & tenon).
Carcase construction
Box built from panels joined end-to-end (lap joints).
One-off production
Single bespoke product; skilled, expensive.
Batch production
4–50 identical products; jigs; medium skill.
Mass production
1000+ products on a production line; low skill.
Continuous production
Never-stopping production (paper, plywood).
Glass paper
Abrasive paper for wood finishing; multiple grades.
Grit
Abrasive grade number; higher = finer.
Sash clamp
Long clamp for gluing boards together.
